article.title: No Economic Justice
article.author: Dick Price, Sharon Kyle, Nina Turner
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. At the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4 at California State University, Los Angeles, former Ohio State Senator Nina Turner delivered an impassioned keynote that challenged progressive activists to rethink how they approach racial justice, economic inequality, and political power. Her central message was unmistakable: The progressive movement cannot achieve economic justice without confronting racial inequality, and it cannot transform American society without learning how to organize and exercise political power. Speaking to an audience of activists, organizers, and community leaders, Turner connected today's struggles to generations of Black freedom fighters who understood that liberation required more than electing sympathetic politicians. It required changing the institutions and economic arrangements that determine whose lives matter and whose needs are ignored. The fourth annual Left Coast Forum was held October 2–4, 2026, at Cal State LA. Recorded by Myla Reason. Learn more at LeftCoastForum.com. Black Liberation Is Central to Everyone's Liberation One of Turner's most consequential arguments concerned the foundational role of Black liberation in American struggles for justice. "You cannot have a class consciousness without having a race consciousness," she declared. Turner challenged progressives who believe that economic inequality can be addressed independently of the country's racial hierarchy. She argued that the Black freedom struggle helped establish the conditions under which women, immigrants, LGBTQ communities, and other marginalized groups could advance their own demands for equality. "Anytime black people have moved for liberation, we have moved for everybody," Turner said. "But sometimes everybody doesn't move for us." Her message was not that other communities' struggles are unimportant. Rather, she maintained that America's particular history of enslavement, white supremacy, and racial domination makes Black liberation essential to understanding the larger struggle for democracy. She urged progressives of every background to recognize that history and choose which side of the struggle their actions support. Political Power Is Meaningless Unless It Is Used Turner also delivered a sharp critique of the Democratic establishment. Although fiercely critical of President Donald Trump, she argued that his administration demonstrates something Democrats should recognize: Political power can be exercised decisively when those holding it are determined to act. "So, when the next Democrat gets in, don't let them tell us what they can't do," she told the audience. For Turner, the question is not simply who wins an election but whose interests government serves once that election is over. She challenged Democrats who promise transformative policies during campaigns but later explain why those promises cannot be fulfilled. "This is about power," she said. "Who it is used for and who it is used against." Her criticism extended to U.S. foreign policy, including American involvement in Gaza and the suffering of civilians in Sudan, Congo, Haiti, and Cuba. She insisted that progressives must apply consistent moral standards regardless of which political party occupies the White House. An Economic Bill of Rights for the 21st Century Turner placed economic inequality at the center of her vision for reconstruction. Quoting Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis, she reminded the audience of the fundamental tension between democracy and concentrated wealth: "We may have democracy or we may have wealth concentrated in the hands of a few. But we cannot have both." She pointed to Franklin D. Roosevelt's proposed Economic Bill of Rights and the Freedom Budget associated with A. Philip Randolph, Bayard Rustin, and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. as examples of ambitious efforts to make economic security a national commitment. Turner acknowledged that Roosevelt's policies were compromised by concessions to white supremacy, particularly the exclusion of many Black workers from early New Deal protections. Nevertheless, she argued that the economic vision of earlier generations remains relevant. Among the policies she advocated were Medicare for All, expanded Social Security, restoration of the expanded child tax credit, a federal employment guarantee, and changes in taxation that would shift more responsibility toward the extremely wealthy. She also proposed redirecting resources from military spending toward meeting human needs. "We can't war our way to peace," Turner declared. With artificial intelligence threatening to disrupt employment, she argued that government must assume greater responsibility for ensuring that technological advancement benefits working people rather than simply concentrating more wealth. From Resistance to Reconstruction Turner's closing message spoke directly to the Left Coast Forum's theme, From Resistance to Reconstruction . She urged progressives to stop allowing disagreements over every issue to prevent cooperation on the issues where common ground already exists. "Even if we don't always agree, my God, for the love of God, can we just pick two or three things?" Building political power, she argued, requires organizing beyond individual campaigns, holding elected officials accountable, and recognizing that everyone has a role to play. Her appeal was also deeply personal. Speaking about her son and grandchildren, Turner explained that she wants every family's children to have the same opportunities she wants for her own. Invoking Congresswoman Barbara Jordan, she reminded the audience that Americans want a country that lives up to its promises. And she closed by emphasizing that political transformation demands participation and sacrifice. Not everyone can contribute equally, but everyone can contribute something. The Left Coast Forum was created to bring progressives together, encourage connections across movements, and help turn those connections into collective action. Turner's keynote offered a challenge consistent with that mission: Building a more just society requires more than resisting injustice. It requires confronting the structures that produce inequality, developing shared goals, and organizing the power necessary to reconstruct them.
